6.text: The mountain-sheep is very cautious, and lives only on rugged mountains.

7.text: When caught on the plain, it immediately makes for the nearest hill, however

8.text: low and easy to climb. In this case the dogs hold the sheep at bay, and

9.text: the hunter is able to catch it with his lasso.

10.text: Of fur-bearing animals, the most important are the white and the red

11.text: fox. The former are much more numerous, though the red variety also lives

12.text: all along the Arctic and Pacific coasts, and is even met with and killed on

13.text: the sea-ice while searching for young seals, or picking up bones left over from

14.text: the feast of the polar bear. The Maritime and Reindeer Chukchee have

15.text: several methods of hunting the fox. The most simple is to run it down on

16.text: a sledge with a swift team of dogs or reindeer. The best hunting-time is

17.text: after the first snow has fallen, which discloses every trace of the animal, and

18.text: makes it hard for it to escape. Swift reindeer are able to overtake a fox

19.text: after two or three hours of hard pursuit. When accustomed to that kind of

20.text: hunting, they become so excited that they try to trample the fox down. The

21.text: reindeer is also used in hunting down the wolf, and will be just as eager to

22.text: catch it and to strike it on the head with the hoof. In fox-hunting the rein-

23.text: deer-driver often does not rely exclusively on the swiftness of his team, but sends

24.text: a hunting-dog after the fox, replacing it by another when the run has lasted

25.text: for a couple of hours (a dog-driver simply releases the swiftest dogs of his

26.text: team one after another for the purpose: the fresh dog will be sure to catch

27.text: the tired animal). When possible, the fox leads the pursuit to some large

28.text: lake where the ice keeps bare of snow for a long time, and therefore is too

29.text: slippery for the reindeer. The short feet of the fox, on such ground, give it

30.text: advantage even over the dog, facilitating sudden turns and retreats. A good

31.text: dog, however, would not give in, but would obstinately keep on with the

32.text: pursuit. Sometimes the two adversaries are so tired that they lie down on

33.text: the ice opposite each other, and rest for a couple of minutes, keeping a close

34.text: watch on each other’s motions. An old wily fox, when pursued, does not go

35.text: into its burrow, for it knows that it can be dug out from the shallow ground

36.text: with but little difficulty. On the Arctic shore the crust of the unfrozen soil

37.text: is so thin, that the ramifications of the burrow extend directly under the sur-

38.text: face, and sometimes the roof can be broken in simply with the foot. Foxes,

39.text: therefore, often prefer to lodge in hollow logs of driftwood or among stones

40.text: rather than burrow in the ground. If the fox is in the burrow, the hunter

41.text: often enlarges the entrance with an axe or an ice-pick; then the fox is extri-

42.text: cated with a split stick that catches in some of the hair of its coat, or even

43.text: simply with the hands, the animal having been dazed with smoke beforehand.
